bib.title: Foundation Models for Decision Making: Problems, Methods, and Opportunities

read.skipped: Reference list (pp. 23-32, from char ~78000) skimmed only for lineage; no appendix.

question: How can foundation models be used within sequential decision making (behavior models, world models, representation learners, agents and environments), and what problems remain open?
hypothesis: Research on foundation models and interactive decision making can be mutually beneficial if considered jointly.
contributions: Scope the problem space of foundation models for decision making
Provide technical tools (MDP, imitation learning, RL, planning background) for understanding current work
Review challenges and open problems and speculate on solutions

results.claim: Tool use by LLM agents is a sequential decision problem like dialogue, but the agent must also decide when to call a tool, which tool, and how to reformulate queries.
results.quote: tool-using agents need to additionally decide when to call external tools, which tools to use, and how to use these tools (e.g., reformulating query if results are not helpful)

results.claim: Supervised finetuning for tool use needs heavy API-call annotation; prompting-based tool use needs hand-crafted prompts per tool and a rule-based parser.
results.quote: the supervised finetuning of tool-use agents requires significant human supervision through API call annotations

results.claim: No existing work considers tool use in an interactive setting where the agent iterates on tool feedback (as of March 2023).
results.quote: none of the existing work considers tool use in an interactive setting where an agent can iterate on its behavior according to tool feedback to improve its tool-use ability

results.claim: RLHF is described as three stages: finetune on dialogue, train a preference model from human rankings, then policy-gradient against it.
results.quote: first, a pretrained language model is finetuned on dialogue data to provide an initial policy

results.claim: Human-feedback-only finetuning leaves failure modes (stale info, hallucination, weak maths); tools giving automatic feedback are argued to be more scalable.
results.quote: leveraging tools and external entities that can automatically provide feedback is likely to be a more scalable and reliable approach

results.claim: Iterative prompting is cast as an MDP with the prompt provider as agent and the LLM as environment; reasoning reward is 1 if the goal answer is reached, else 0.
results.quote: R(𝑠𝑡,𝑎𝑡) = 1 if the language model’s output successfully reaches a goal answer

results.claim: Prompting schemes are cast as high-level actions (DECOMPOSE, RANK, DENOISE, PARAPHRASE) that compose recursively.
results.quote: such high-level actions include DECOMPOSE [Press et al. 2022], RANK [Kumar and Talukdar 2021], DENOISE [Shi et al. 2023], and PARAPHRASE

results.claim: Generalist transformer agents cover over 40 Atari games, over 700 robot tasks, over 600 tasks (Gato).
results.source: Lee et al. 2022; Brohan et al. 2022; Reed et al. 2022
results.quote: over 40 Atari games [Lee et al. 2022], over 700 real-world robot tasks [Brohan et al. 2022], and over 600 distinct tasks

results.claim: Training a single Atari game from scratch with prior sequential decision methods takes 7 GPU days.
results.quote: requiring 7 GPU days of interactive game-play to solve a single Atari game

results.claim: Algorithm Distillation adapts in context purely, without updating network parameters; corrective re-prompting feeds environment errors back as prompts.
results.source: Laskin et al. 2022; Raman et al. 2022
results.quote: adapts to downstream tasks purely in-context without updating any network parameters

results.claim: Open problem: bounded context length and need for external memory/retrieval for long-horizon decision making.
results.quote: existing approaches typically rely on transformers that have a bounded context length

results.claim: Language models with auxiliary memory are said to emulate universal Turing machines, so LLMs could act as computers programmed by prompting.
results.quote: language models with auxiliary memory have been shown to emulate universal Turing machines

results.claim: Software tools (search engines, databases, compilers) as environments give scalable online access, enabling RL finetuning of LLM policies.
results.quote: language models as interactive agents enables massive online access to environments that are highly scalable and available (e.g., search engines, databases, compilers)

limits: Survey/position report of March 2023 with no experiments; no benchmark numbers of its own.
Authors concede tool-use agents have no interactive iteration on tool feedback and text-as-environment has a substantial gap to task-specific game solvers.
Much has dated: it predates ReAct-style agent loops, function calling and agentic RL at scale, so the open problems in 5.2 and 6.4 have been partly addressed.
practices: Treat tool use as sequential decision making with API responses as feedback (5.2).
Prefer tool or environment feedback over human feedback alone for properties like factuality and calculation (5.1).
Treat tools such as browsers as interactive environments and optimise queries with RL (5.2).
Use language as a universal interface for task specification and environment description (6.2).
Handle long context with summarise/prune/search prompting actions and external memory (5.3, 6.3).

terms.definition: a conversation τ<t consists of sentences produced by agent π and human environment E; state is the history, action the agent response
iterative prompting as interaction between a prompt provider π and a language model environment E
sequence models generating next states without respecting environment transitions
also known as skills or options; composable behaviours modelled from diverse interactive data
the broad datasets from vision and language D and the task specific interactive datasets D_RL can be of distinct modalities and structures
